1. Why People Explore
2. The Traveller Who Went Everywhere
3. The Great Fleets of China
4. Sailing into the Unknown

explorer: a person who travels to find out about unknown places
caravan: a group travelling together, often across desert
fleet: a large group of ships
voyage: a long journey by sea
continent: one of the Earth's great land masses
Antarctica: the frozen continent at the far south

What makes a person leave everything they know and set off towards a place on no map? For some it was gold, or trade, or the fame of being first. For others it was something simpler and harder to name: the need to know what lies over the next hill. That need is very old, and very human.

image.note: A lone figure on a ridge at dawn looking towards distant unknown mountains; small against a wide world

pages.text: We often think of explorers as men from Europe in tall ships. Some were. But the greatest travellers of the old world came from many lands, and some of the boldest set out from Africa and Asia long before the European ships were built. Let us meet a few of them.

image.note: A gallery of diverse travellers: an African scholar on camel, a Chinese admiral, a European captain; equal in size

pages.text: Seven hundred years ago, a young man from Morocco named Ibn Battuta set out to make one journey. He did not stop for nearly thirty years. He crossed the whole Sahara, sailed the coast of East Africa, reached India and China, and travelled roughly seventy-five thousand miles, farther than almost anyone before him.

image.note: Ibn Battuta on camelback crossing a vast desert, a caravan behind him; heat shimmer, adventure

pages.text: When he finally came home, a ruler asked him to tell his story, and a great book was written down from it. Because of that book, we can still read what the world looked like through the eyes of a curious African traveller centuries ago. He explored not to conquer, but to see, and to tell.

image.note: Ibn Battuta dictating his travels to a scribe, both leaning over a table; storytelling

pages.text: At about the same time, on the other side of the world, China built the largest ships the world had ever seen. An admiral named Zheng He led huge fleets across the Indian Ocean, reaching Arabia and the coast of East Africa. His treasure ships were so vast that the little European ships of later years would have looked like toys beside them.

image.note: A giant Chinese treasure ship dwarfing smaller boats; nine masts, red sails; awe

pages.text: Zheng He's fleets carried silk and porcelain to trade, and brought wonders home. On one voyage they returned with a giraffe from Africa, which amazed the whole imperial court. For a while, China ruled the seas. Exploring, the world learned, was never the invention of one people alone.

image.note: A giraffe being led into a Chinese royal court, astonished officials; gentle humour, wonder

pages.text: Then came the age when Europe took to the oceans. Sailors like Vasco da Gama found a sea route around Africa to India. Christopher Columbus, hoping to reach Asia, sailed west and instead reached lands in the Americas he had never expected. These voyages joined up the world as never before.

image.note: A small wooden caravel on a huge empty ocean under a big sky; brave and tiny

pages.text: But we must be honest about these journeys. The lands the European sailors "discovered" were not empty. Millions of people already lived there, with their own cities and histories. For those people, the arrival of the ships often brought great suffering. An explorer to one side of the sea can be an invader to the other.

image.note: A ship arriving offshore while a settled coastal people watch warily from the shore; wary, not welcoming

pages.text: Ferdinand Magellan set out to do the boldest thing of all: to sail all the way around the whole world. He himself died on the journey, but a few of his men struggled home years later, the first people ever to circle the Earth. They proved beyond doubt that the world was round, and that every sea joined every other.

image.note: A battered ship limping into harbour with a thin, weary crew; survival, not glory

chapters.title: To the Ends of the Earth

pages.text: When the coasts were all mapped, explorers turned to the hardest places left. Some crossed burning deserts. Some pushed into thick rainforests. And some set their eyes on the coldest place on Earth, the frozen continent of Antarctica, where no one lived and almost nothing could.

image.note: A tiny line of figures hauling sledges across an endless white ice sheet; brutal, vast

pages.text: The race to reach the South Pole was fierce and deadly. A Norwegian team led by Roald Amundsen reached it first, carefully and well prepared. A British team led by Robert Scott reached it soon after, but died on the way back through cold and hunger. The lesson was hard: courage is not enough. You must also plan.

image.note: A flag planted at the South Pole in howling wind; two sets of tracks; solemn

pages.text: You might think there is nothing left to explore. You would be wrong. The deep ocean floor is less mapped than the surface of the Moon. Machines are crawling across the red deserts of Mars right now. Somewhere, a scientist is naming a creature no human has ever seen.

image.note: Split image: a deep-sea submersible in dark water; a rover on Mars; both lit by their own lamps

pages.text: And the explorers of tomorrow are children today, perhaps reading this very book. You do not need a ship or a sledge. You need the oldest tool of all, the one every great traveller carried: the itch to find out, and the courage to go and look. The map is not finished. Some of it is waiting for you.

image.note: A modern Nigerian child looking up at the stars from an estate rooftop, a telescope beside them; hopeful
